scenario: Today’s retrieval track asks where retrieval should be spent, how relevance should be judged, and how a new model can keep using an old index. Large-scale relevance labels need not come from one large-model call per document; a program written for each topic can stay close to human assessment. Allocating a retrieval budget by closed-book confidence mainly pays off when passages are scarce, or when retrieval may overwrite a known answer, and it barely helps choose how deep to read. Search-augmented models should still credit useful evidence when every answer is wrong. An encoder can be upgraded without re-encoding the whole gallery, and a compact, diverse in-house store can take minimal retrieval augmentation onto reasoning-intensive benchmarks. Documents in a cache have to be reusable at a new position, and autoformalization first has to find the right formal definition of a concept in the mathematical library.

papers.title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
papers.authors: Eugene Agichtein, Charles L. A. Clarke, Kaustubh Dhole, William Stern
papers.summary: Labeling retrieval results with a large language model usually means one expensive frontier-model call per document, and the labels are hard to interpret or reproduce. A practical alternative is to let the model write a readable program for each topic, then grade the whole pool with that program. The programs rely only on lexical matching, standard natural-language libraries, and pool statistics; if a few human labels are available, the rules can be adjusted once more. On seven TREC collections, the unlabeled programs agree with NIST assessors at the level of Claude Sonnet 5.5 judges on recent deep-learning tracks. The labels rank official TREC runs with Kendall’s τ between 0.87 and 0.94, and writing the programs is a one-time cost with no further interface calls for grading. For teams that must label deep result pools, ==an inspectable, reproducible program can sometimes replace a per-document model judge.==
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our resul
papers.score_note: 用可执行 program judge 替代 LLM judge 做规模化相关性标注，直接服务搜索评价。有明确问题与方法，证据在摘要中称可扩展高效，证据记 4。

papers.title: Doubling Query Embedding Throughput with Dynamic Batching in Vespa Cloud
papers.summary: As query volume grows, every query must pass through an embedding model, and running each request on its own uses a GPU inefficiently, so throughput and latency both suffer under heavy load. Open-source Vespa, and Vespa Cloud until now, ran each embedding request as a separate inference call, so launch overhead and memory use stacked up as concurrency rose. A new cloud inference runtime on container nodes adds dynamic batching, combining concurrent requests into batches and limiting how many calls run at once. On an NVIDIA L4, query throughput for EmbeddingGemma 2 rises from about 300 to about 600 queries per second, while median latency stays at 15 milliseconds. Dynamic batching therefore lets the same GPU absorb about twice the query load at nearly unchanged median latency, so fewer GPU nodes are needed for the same query rate. The capability is already available on container nodes in Vespa Cloud.
papers.abstract: Vespa Cloud now supports dynamic batching of concurrent requests for local embedding models. In our benchmarks, this more than doubles the number of queries embedded per second on a GPU, while adding just a few milliseconds of latency at low loads.
papers.score_note: Vespa Cloud 动态 batching，查询 embedding 吞吐翻倍、中位延迟几乎不变（EmbeddingGemma 2 约 300→600 q/s；Arctic 约 450→900 q/s）。2026-11-18 工业实践，覆盖度必选。

papers.title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
papers.authors: Wen Wang, Jindong Wang, Jiahua Bao, Tu Yongsiqi, Yihao Liu, Junwei He, Wenkui Fan
papers.summary: Search-augmented language models often learn from the final answer alone, so a useful search and a useless one receive the same credit when the answer is wrong. Advantages also collapse to zero when every sampled rollout fails. Evidence-based credit assignment adds a training-only signal: a frozen copy of the current policy is queried with just the question and the documents seen so far, measuring how much those passages raise the likelihood of a reference answer. Across seven search-question benchmarks, the variant that keeps the full evidence gain raises strict macro exact match over outcome-only GRPO by 1.03 percentage points on a 3-billion-parameter model and by 4.80 percentage points on a 7-billion-parameter model. In all-failure rollout groups, it also recovers a nonzero learning signal in the great majority of groups. ==A wrong final answer does not mean the search provided no useful evidence.==
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts
papers.score_note: Tencent：为 search-augmented LM 做基于证据的 credit assignment。今晨 OAI 有记录但预过滤漏掉，Step 2 回收。核心 AI 搜索。

papers.title: Know Before You Fetch: When Does Confidence-Based Retrieval-Budget Allocation Pay Off?
papers.authors: Zhe Dong, Fang Qin, Manish Shah
papers.summary: Deciding whether and how deeply to retrieve from closed-book confidence is usually compared with always fetching many passages, which leaves out cheaper fixed depths or random mixtures. This work compares confidence-based allocation with the best simple policy under the same cap on average passages per query, allowing only zero, one, or five passages. In all seven settings, when the cap is half a passage per query, the adaptive policy beats the best simple policy by 0.010 to 0.075 in accuracy. At caps of one passage or more, substantial gains appear almost only on Wikipedia, where passages often overwrite answers the reader already knew. Confidence ranks whether a first passage helps, but barely ranks the choice between one and five passages. Once the probe’s latency is also charged, gains often remain only when the gate skips retrieval for most queries. ==Confidence-based budgets mainly pay off when passages are scarce, or when retrieval can spoil a known answer.==
papers.abstract: Adaptive retrieval-augmented generation uses a signal from the reader, such as its confidence when answering without retrieval (closed-book), to decide whether and how much to retrieve. We compare such methods not with always retrieving many passages but with the best simple policy under the same cap on average passages per query: a fixed depth or a random mixture of fixed depths. Policies allocate zero, one or five passages and are scored on held-out questions. Seven settings of about 2,000 questions combine TriviaQA, Natural Questions and MS MARCO, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B readers, and two retrieval sources: per-question passage pools and a 3.5-million-passage Wikipedia index. Allocation by confidence could gain in three ways. It rations a scarce budget: at a cap of half a passage per query it beats the best simple policy in all seven settings, by 0.010 to 0.075 in accuracy. papers.score_note: Know Before You Fetch：置信度驱动的检索预算分配，RAG 效率。OAI 于 2026-11-19 再公告，Step 2 回收。

papers.title: MIRAGE: A Framework for Multi-hop Reasoning under Dynamic Knowledge Injection
papers.authors: Heyang Xu, HanWen Hao, Haifeng Wang, Haoyi Zhou, Jianxin Li
papers.summary: When multi-hop question answering must absorb both conflicting knowledge updates and entirely new facts, errors often come from trusting the wrong source at a given hop: the model clings to outdated parametric memory, or cannot answer when the fact is new. A new benchmark covers both conflict and incremental knowledge, and a training-free framework routes each hop by the model’s probability that its own answer is true, then uses a light template to correct leftover structural mistakes. On that benchmark, GPT-4o with a single edit raises accuracy from 52.15% for the comparison method to 73.65%. On a separate edited multi-hop set, the method also recovers about 96% of the unedited reference accuracy. For multi-hop reasoning under ongoing knowledge injection, ==deciding which source to trust at each hop often matters more than only retrieving the new documents.==
papers.abstract: Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and synthesize multiple pieces of evidence into a coherent reasoning path, which is essential for complex tasks. However, prior work on knowledge updating for MQA has largely focused on simple fact edits, overlooking a more challenging and realistic setting---\emph{Knowledge Injection}---in which the model must simultaneously accommodate both conflicting updates and entirely novel information. Under this setting, a hop-level answer is often wrong simply because the model trusts the wrong knowledge source: it clings to outdated parametric memory when the injected knowledge conflicts with it (K2), and it cannot answer when the required fact is entirely new (K3). To investigate this, we introduce NEXUS, the first benchmark tailored for multi-hop reasoning under Knowledge Injection, which explicitly covers both conflicting (K2) and incremental (K3) knowledge. papers.score_note: MIRAGE：动态知识注入下的多跳推理框架，信息寻求。

papers.title: VIBRA: Backward-Compatible Cross-Modal Retrieval with Consensus Barycenters
papers.authors: Shubing Yang, Xutong Liu, Dongfang Zhao
papers.summary: When a cross-modal retriever is upgraded, a new encoder cannot query a gallery already encoded by the old model unless billions of items are re-encoded. Existing compatible methods either stay near the old model’s accuracy or run both encoders for every query. A new method matches relevance on the old gallery, corrects single-model errors with the barycenter of several views as a query in the old space, and trains the new encoder to inherit that consensus, so models absent at deployment still shape every query. Across all upgrade settings among five benchmarks and six backbones, it is the best compatible method. Recall@1 rises by up to 5.6 points over the strongest baseline and by up to 18.0 points over the old model, while adding less than 1 millisecond of latency to the new encoder. ==A compatible upgrade need not choose between accuracy and running two encoders per query.==
papers.abstract: Backward-compatible retrieval enables a new encoder to query the gallery that an old model has already encoded, so that a cross-modal retrieval system can be upgraded without re-encoding billions of items. Existing compatible methods either fit the old query and stay near the accuracy of the old model, or run the old and the new encoder for every query. We propose VIBRA, which matches relevance on the old gallery, corrects the errors of a single model with the barycenter of several views, which is itself a query in the old space, and trains the new encoder to inherit this consensus, so that models absent at deployment still shape every query. We show that the barycenter gains margin over the average of its views exactly when their hardest irrelevant items differ, and we characterize the share of this gain that one encoder can reach. On five benchmarks with five upgrades among six CLIP, MetaCLIP and SigLIP2 backbones, VIBRA is the best compatible method in all 50 settings, improving Rec
papers.score_note: VIBRA：向后兼容的跨模态检索。

papers.title: Frustratingly Simple Retrieval Improves Challenging, Reasoning-Intensive Benchmarks
papers.authors: Xinxi Lyu, Michael Duan, Rulin Shao, Pang Wei Koh, Sewon Min
papers.summary: Minimal retrieval-augmented generation is often thought to help little, or even to hurt, on reasoning-intensive benchmarks. What is missing is often not a more complex agent pipeline, but a usable web-scale datastore whose coverage is closer to pretraining data. A compact, high-quality store filters out most web pages, then combines in-memory approximate nearest-neighbor search with exact search on disk, reaching subsecond latency on a single node. Plugged into a minimal retrieval-augmented pipeline, models of various sizes improve consistently on every tested benchmark, with relative gains of 33% on MMLU Pro and 19% on MATH. No single data source suffices alone. The in-house store matches or outperforms Google Search across all benchmarks, and is competitive with recent, more complex agent-based retrieval systems, while staying simple, reproducible, and self-contained.
papers.abstract: Retrieval augmentation has primarily been studied in limited settings, such as factoid question answering; more challenging, reasoning-intensive benchmarks have seen limited success from minimal RAG. In this work, we challenge this prevailing view on a set of established, reasoning-intensive benchmarks: MMLU, MMLU Pro, AGI Eval, GPQA, and MATH. We identify a key missing component in prior work: a usable, web-scale datastore aligned with the breadth of pretraining data. To this end, we introduce CompactDS: a diverse, high-quality, web-scale datastore that achieves high retrieval accuracy and subsecond latency on a single-node deployment, making it suitable for academic use. Its core design combines a compact set of high-quality, diverse data sources with in-memory approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) retrieval and on-disk exact search. Using CompactDS, a minimal RAG pipeline achieves consistent accuracy improvements across all benchmarks and model sizes (8B--70B), with relative gains of 1
papers.score_note: Frustratingly Simple Retrieval 提升困难推理基准，方法朴素但与检索相关。

papers.title: LazyAttention: Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Deferred Positional Encoding
papers.authors: Haocheng Xia, Mihir Pamnani, Hanxi Fang, Supawit Chockchowwat, Yongjoo Park
papers.summary: Key-value caching speeds up long-context inference, but conventional caches write positional information in, so the same document is hard to reuse directly at a new position. In retrieval-augmented generation, hot documents recur across requests and in different orders, yet they cannot share a cache once their positions change. Existing fixes either reuse only prefixes or materialize the cache again to re-encode positions, which is expensive. An attention mechanism that defers positional encoding adjusts positions inside the kernel on the fly, so one physical key-value copy can serve many logical requests at arbitrary positions. Under skewed document access, relative to the strongest Block-Attention baseline, it reduces time to the first token by 1.37 times and raises inference throughput by 1.40 times, with comparable output quality. ==Positions need not be written into the cache first, so retrieved documents are easier to share across requests.==
papers.abstract: Key-value (KV) caching accelerates inference of large language models (LLMs) by reusing past computations for generated tokens. Its importance becomes even greater in long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and in-context learning (ICL). However, conventional KV caching embeds positional information directly into the cache, limiting its reusability. Existing solutions either restrict reuse to prefixes or require expensive memory materialization for positional re-encoding. We introduce LazyAttention, a novel attention mechanism that kernelizes deferred positional encoding to enable zero-copy, position-agnostic KV reuse. By adjusting positional encoding within attention kernels on-the-fly, LazyAttention resolves the materialization bottleneck, allowing a single physical KV copy to serve multiple logical requests at arbitrary positions. papers.score_note: LazyAttention：延迟位置编码的高效 RAG。

papers.title: Rankify: A Comprehensive Python Toolkit for Retrieval, Re-Ranking, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Abdelrahman Abdallah, Bhawna Piryani, Jamshid Mozafari, Andreas Herzinger, Jamie Holdcroft
papers.summary: Building a retrieval-augmented generation system often means stitching together separate tools for retrieval, reranking, and generation, with incompatible data formats, evaluation pipelines, and deployment workflows that make systematic comparison hard. An open-source Python toolkit unifies the three stages in one modular framework, offering dozens of benchmarks with pre-retrieved documents and ready-made indices, more than ten retrievers, more than twenty rerankers, and several generation strategies and inference backends. The authors run more than two hundred configurations on question-answering as well as BEIR and TREC benchmarks. Across those configurations, adding a reranker raises downstream exact match by 5 to 15 percentage points regardless of retriever or generator, and context precision rises by up to 8.5 points. For anyone comparing a retrieval stack, ==a unified interface is itself what makes the value of reranking measurable.==
papers.abstract: Abdelrahman Abdallah, Bhawna Piryani, Jamshid Mozafari, Andreas Herzinger, Jamie Holdcroft, Adam Jatowt. Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3: System Demonstrations). 2026.
papers.score_note: Rankify：检索/重排/RAG 工具包，新颖性低、实用性高。

papers.title: Automated Formalization via Conceptual Retrieval-Augmented LLMs
papers.authors: Wangyue Lu, Lun Du, Sirui Li, Ke Weng, Haozhe Sun, Hengyu Liu, Minghe Yu, Tiancheng Zhang, Ge Yu
papers.summary: When natural-language mathematical theorems are automatically written as formal code, models often invent predicates that are not in the library, misuse symbols, or mix up the same concept as defined in different domains. A concept-driven retrieval-augmented framework automatically builds a concept-to-definition knowledge base from Lean’s standard mathematical library, covering more than twenty-six thousand formal definitions and more than a thousand core concepts. It then uses query expansion with domain and application cues and a dual-channel hybrid retriever to fetch the formal definitions that ground generation, and it can be plugged into existing large-model autoformalization pipelines. On standard benchmarks and a new, more demanding set, translation accuracy improves by up to 62.1% and by 29.9% on average, in relative terms. ==Finding the right formal definition of a concept is what cuts hallucination and cross-domain confusion.==
papers.abstract: Interactive theorem provers (ITPs) require manual formalization, which is labor-intensive and demands expert knowledge. While automated formalization offers a potential solution, it faces two major challenges: model hallucination (e.g., undefined predicates, symbol misuse, and version incompatibility) and the semantic gap caused by ambiguous or missing premises in natural language descriptions. To address these issues, we propose CRAMF, a Concept-driven Retrieval-Augmented Mathematical Formalization framework. CRAMF enhances LLM-based autoformalization by retrieving formal definitions of core mathematical concepts, providing contextual grounding during code generation. However, applying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this setting is non-trivial due to the lack of structured knowledge bases, the polymorphic nature of mathematical concepts, and the high precision required in formal retrieval.
